title: Pipeline Anatomy: Build → Test → Package → Deploy
objectives: Name the stages of a delivery pipeline and what each one produces
Order stages to fail fast and cache dependencies without poisoning builds
Read a GitHub Actions-style YAML: jobs, steps, needs, artifacts, cache
Promote one immutable artifact through environments instead of rebuilding per stage
body:
Every hand-run release is a ritual waiting to be forgotten under pressure: which branch, which tests, did we tag, was that the staging build? A pipeline encodes the ritual once, runs it identically on every commit, and refuses to skip steps when someone is in a hurry.

## The problem

Constraints that shape every pipeline: feedback must be fast (a 40-minute CI is a CI people route around), builds must be reproducible (the artifact you tested is the artifact you ship), and failures must stop promotion early. Those three constraints imply the classic shape.

## The stages

- **Build** — compile/bundle, produce an artifact (dist/, a binary, a Docker image). Fails on syntax and type errors.
- **Test** — unit first (seconds), then integration (database, containers). Gate: no green, no artifact moves forward.
- **Package** — turn the artifact into the deployable unit: a versioned, tagged container image pushed to a registry.
- **Deploy** — run it somewhere real, behind a health gate. Failure here means rollback, not shrug.

Each stage consumes the previous stage's output. That chaining — needs: in Actions — is what makes 'tested == shipped' true. Rebuilding the image per environment breaks that chain: staging and prod can silently differ, and the pipeline proves nothing.

## Failing fast

Order by cost: lint and typecheck (seconds) before unit tests (minutes) before integration (minutes more) before build/package. If the typecheck fails, nobody waits for the integration suite. The same logic keeps integration jobs split from unit jobs so a flaky external dependency cannot block fast feedback for every developer.

## Caching dependencies

Dependency download is the most cacheable, most repeated cost. Cache keyed on the lockfile hash:

```yaml
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.npm
    key: npm-${{ hashFiles('package-lock.json') }}
```

Same lockfile → restore in seconds. Never cache node_modules into an artifact or a Docker layer COPYed forward — caches speed builds; they must not become part of what you ship. Inside Dockerfiles, the same principle is the manifest-before-source COPY order.

## A concrete pipeline (GitHub Actions style)

```yaml
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --coverage

  package:
    needs: test                       # the gate
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy-staging:
    needs: package
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh staging ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }}
```

Three jobs, chained by needs. The image is tagged with the commit SHA — immutable, traceable, and the exact thing tested is the exact thing deployed. Secrets enter only as injected variables, never in the YAML.

## Artifacts and promotion

Build once, promote the artifact: the SHA-tagged image flows test → staging → production unchanged; only configuration (env vars, secrets, replicas) differs per environment. If fixing an environment requires a rebuild, that is a defect in the pipeline, because the new artifact has by definition not been through the gates the old one passed.

## Best practices

- Fast checks first; keep unit and integration jobs separate.
- needs as the only path to production — no manual side doors.
- Tag images with the commit SHA (plus a semver when releasing); deploy by digest or immutable tag.
- Cache dependencies keyed on lockfiles; never ship cached node_modules.
- Keep pipeline YAML in the repo, reviewed like code.
- Gated deploys with a health check before calling success.

## Common mistakes

- One giant job: a typo makes you re-run the 30-minute suite from scratch.
- use: true in cache keys without the lockfile hash — caches go stale and builds break mysteriously.
- Rebuilding the image per environment, destroying the tested-shipped equivalence.
- Secrets pasted into YAML or logs; they belong in the platform's secret store.
- Skip-on-red culture: allowing deploy when tests fail — the pipeline's only real job.

examples.name: pipeline.yml
examples.code:
name: ci
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm            # keyed on package-lock.json internally
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint       # fail fast: seconds
      - run: npm test           # gate for packaging

  package:
    needs: test                 # no green tests -> no image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.REGISTRY_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/acme/api:latest   # convenience only; deploy by SHA

  deploy-staging:
    needs: package
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: staging
    steps:
      - run: ./deploy.sh staging ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }}

# Anatomy:
#   test -> package -> deploy-staging, chained by needs
#   one artifact (sha-tagged image) promoted, never rebuilt per env
#   secrets injected from the platform store, absent from YAML

exercise.prompt: Simulate pipeline gating in JavaScript. runPipeline(jobs, artifacts) returns the summary: for each job in order, skipped or ok or failed, and whether the final deploy happened. A job with failed dependencies is skipped; a failed job stops all downstream work. Bonus: add the gate result for a flaky test run included in the input. Render the summary.
hints: Process jobs in dependency order; keep a map of each job's outcome as you go.
A need that is failed OR skipped means the job is skipped too — skipped propagates.
deployed is true only when every job finished ok.

questions.prompt: Why should lint/typecheck run before the integration test suite?
options: They are more important than tests
They fail in seconds, so cheap failures stop the pipeline before the expensive stages run
Integration tests cannot fail on a type error
questions.explanation: Fail fast is an ordering principle: cheapest, most-deterministic checks first, so broken commits get feedback in seconds instead of after a 20-minute suite.

questions.prompt: Why build ONE sha-tagged image and promote it through environments, instead of rebuilding per environment?
options: The tested artifact and the deployed artifact stay byte-identical; rebuilds break that guarantee
Rebuilt images are slower to pull
questions.explanation: Promotion preserves 'what you tested is what you ship'. A rebuild can pull newer dependencies or pick up uncommitted differences, silently invalidating every green gate.

questions.prompt: In the sample pipeline, what does needs: test on the package job guarantee?
options: The jobs run on the same runner
package cannot start until test succeeds — failed tests block packaging
package re-runs the tests in parallel
test artifacts are deleted after packaging
questions.explanation: needs is the dependency gate: no green test run, no packaging, and therefore nothing deployable — the pipeline's entire point.
